paper.title: The Unintended Consequences of Rebalancing
paper.paper_claim: A 60/40 calendar-rebalancing signal negatively predicts next-day equity-minus-bond returns near month-end. A one-standard-deviation decrease in the Calendar signal is associated with about +17 bp equity return and -2.4 bp bond return over the next trading day.

hypothesis: A simple point-in-time 60/40 calendar drift signal retains economically useful month-end predictability in the untouched 2026 post-revision period and beats a simpler month-end equity-minus-bond benchmark after execution cost.
acceptance_rule: USE or CONDITION only if the signal has the paper-consistent negative slope and produces positive after-cost event returns while improving return and at least two of volatility, maximum drawdown and Expected Shortfall versus a simple final-business-day long SPY/short BND benchmark. Otherwise REJECT the trading implementation. This run does not reject the paper's market-impact mechanism itself.

data.source: Alpaca Market Data, IEX daily bars
data.missing_value_policy: No forward fill, interpolation or alternate-feed fallback.
data.proxy_limitations: SPY and BND are executable ETF proxies, whereas the paper's main regressions use S&P 500 and 10-year Treasury note futures.

method.signal_time: Close of the trading day immediately before the final business day of each month.
method.signal: Equity weight drift from 60%, computed from close-to-close SPY and BND returns since the previous month-end reset. Positive means equities are overweight.
method.signal_strategy: On the final business day, take -sign(weight drift) exposure to the SPY-minus-BND daily return spread.
method.simple_benchmark: Always long the SPY-minus-BND return spread on the final business day of each month.

predictive_relation.interpretation: Direction is consistent with the paper, but the sample contains only eight post-revision month-end events.

verdict_reason: The 2026 post-revision data preserve the paper-consistent negative relation between 60/40 equity drift and the final-day equity-minus-bond spread, but the sign strategy does not beat the simple benchmark. The signal strategy earns about 1.72% cumulatively before costs and 0.91% after a 10 bp/event drag, versus about 4.66% for always being long the final-day SPY-minus-BND spread. It also has materially worse maximum drawdown and 95% Expected Shortfall. Under the repository rule that added complexity must beat a simple alternative, the trading implementation is rejected.
decision_use: Do not add a calendar-rebalancing front-running strategy to portfolio authority. The paper remains useful as execution-risk evidence: avoid assuming that a fixed, publicly predictable month-end rebalance is costless, and test randomized or wider execution windows before institutional-scale rebalancing.
do_not_use_for: Claiming the original paper is false
Assuming SPY/BND exactly replicate futures-based paper coefficients
Inferring statistical significance from eight events
implementation: Negative evidence only. No strategy code, collector, model or workflow is added.
next_test: Test the decision-relevant execution question rather than the rejected front-running rule: for the portfolio's actual rebalance sizes, compare fixed month-end execution with randomized execution over the final five trading days using executable bid/ask data and market-impact assumptions; adopt only if the randomized schedule lowers realized implementation shortfall without materially increasing allocation drift.
